--- title: "Tuberculosis in Households and the Community" description: "A full TB model on a three-layer contact network: households as cliques built with netclique() and kept intact through births, deaths, and people leaving home, plus regular and casual community contacts as TERGMs. Fast and slow latency, reinfection under partial protection, age-specific natural history, and heavy-tailed infectiousness. It asks why households carry a small share of transmission despite a large share of contact time, how the persistence of ties changes transmission, and what household contact investigation with preventive therapy achieves next to community-wide and random screening." author: "Samuel M. Jenness" date: "2026-09-28" categories: [tuberculosis, multilayer, households, netclique, vital dynamics, age structure, screening, advanced] order: 12 image: thumbnail.png --- ## Overview Tuberculosis (TB) is transmitted through shared air, most often over long periods of contact, and most people infected with *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* never develop disease. Those who do usually progress within the first year or two after infection, a smaller number decades later, and a person with active TB can transmit for many months before diagnosis. In high-burden settings, recent transmission, including reinfection of people already infected, accounts for most incident disease. Household members share more contact time than any other set of people, and household contact investigation, in which the co-residents of every newly diagnosed person are screened for TB and offered preventive treatment, is a core WHO recommendation. Yet molecular and genomic studies in high-burden settings attribute only 8 to 19% of transmission to household contacts ([Verver et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(03)15332-9); [Glynn et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0132840); [Middelkoop et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1093/infdis/jiu403)), and in a Western Cape contact survey households held 36% of adults' contact time but, in a model built on those data, only 13% of disease ([McCreesh and White 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-23797-2)). How much transmission happens at home, and why it is less than contact time suggests, decides how much a household-targeted program can accomplish. This example builds a TB model to examine that question. It has three features that no other Gallery example combines: 1. **A household clique layer in an open population.** Households are cliques built with `netclique()`. Newborns join a household through the layer's arrival rule, the dead leave with their edges, and young adults leave home to form new households through `move_to_group()`. Two TERGM layers carry non-household contacts: *regular* contacts (coworkers, classmates, friends) that last about a year, and *casual* contacts (transport, markets, shops) that are redrawn every month. Each contact layer is weighted by its contact time, taken from a Western Cape contact survey. 2. **A TB natural history with age structure.** The disease states follow the compartmental model of [Rothman et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129174): early (fast) and late (slow) latent infection, reinfection under the partial protection of prior infection, active disease, treatment, and relapse. To these the example adds self-cure, clearance of late latent infection, age-specific progression and infectiousness for children and adults, births and deaths over decades, and heavy-tailed variation in how infectious each case is. 3. **Two experiments that need a network.** *Part 1* holds contact time and per-contact-hour risk fixed and rearranges the same contacts: households as they are, regular contacts redrawn every month, and household contact time spread across random partners redrawn every month. This separates what the *persistence* and clustering of ties do to transmission from what the *amount* of contact does. *Part 2* resumes the baseline and compares household contact investigation, with and without preventive therapy, against community-wide screening of adults and against an equal-effort comparator that screens the same number of people chosen at random, which isolates the value of the household link. The policy question is the one asked of TB programs in high-burden settings: *what does household contact investigation achieve, per person screened and for the population, when most transmission happens outside the home?* ::: {.callout-note} ## EpiModel features used here - `netclique()` for a household layer of cliques, with `arrivals = "join"` and a custom `arrivals.FUN` that places newborns; `assign_groups()` to build households around existing ages; and `move_to_group()` to move people between households during a simulation. - TERGM layers with a fully targeted `nodemix` mixing matrix, and per-layer `control.simulate.formula.tergm()` settings passed with `multilayer()`. - Custom modules with an explicit `module.order`, transmission on each layer weighted by contact-hours, and `set_transmat()` records with extra columns. - A burn-in saved with `save.run = TRUE`, and intervention scenarios resumed from it with `use_scenario()`. - Monte Carlo intervals on every model output. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## How this relates to other TB models The TB models most used for policy, including TIME Impact, Tabby2, AuTuMN, Optima TB, and the models in the TB Modelling and Analysis Consortium comparisons, are population-level compartmental models, as is the [Rothman et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vaccine.2026.129174) model from which this example takes its disease structure. They represent contact through mixing matrices and are built to project incidence, mortality, and costs for a country. Household structure appears in theoretical models of close and casual contact ([Aparicio et al. 2000](https://doi.org/10.1006/jtbi.2000.2129)) and in research individual-based and network models ([Cohen et al. 2007](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2006.0193); [Kasaie et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.201310-1846OC); [McCreesh and White 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-23797-2); [Havumaki et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008713)), nearly all of which hold community ties fixed; one built in EpiModel used static village networks ([Pando et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-023-16425-w)). This example trades calibration to a country for an explicit multilayer network in which households are real groups, community ties turn over at a rate the modeler chooses, and every transmission is attributed to a layer. Its setting is a generic high-burden one without HIV, its parameters are illustrative, and it is not calibrated to surveillance data. Treat it as a template for building a TB network model, not as a projection for any place. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Download and run the standalone scripts - [model.R](model.R): main simulation script - [module-fx.R](module-fx.R): custom module functions `model.R` sources `module-fx.R` from `examples/tuberculosis/` when run from the repository root and from the working directory otherwise. Sourcing the script interactively uses the full settings on this page (`N = 20000`, ten simulations, a 50-year burn-in for each of three contact structures, five 10-year intervention scenarios), which take about half an hour on five cores. `Rscript` is not interactive and uses small continuous-integration settings whose results are not meant to be interpreted; to get the full settings from the command line, pass R code that defines `run_full` as the first argument: ```bash Rscript model.R "run_full <- TRUE" ``` ::: ## Model Structure ### Disease states | Status | Description | Can be infected? | Infectious? | |---|---|---|---| | **s** | Never infected | yes, full susceptibility | no | | **e** | Early latent infection, the months after infection when the risk of disease is highest | no | no | | **l** | Late latent infection, with a small lifelong risk of reactivation | yes, at 21% of full susceptibility | no | | **c** | Infection cleared, spontaneously or by preventive therapy; no risk of reactivation | yes, at 21% of full susceptibility | no | | **i** | Active TB, not yet diagnosed | no | yes, by age and case | | **t** | On treatment (six months) | no | no | | **r** | Recovered from TB (treated or self-cured), with a risk of relapse in the first years | yes, full susceptibility | no | ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false flowchart LR S["s

recovered"] T -->|cure| R T -->|failure or loss| I R -->|relapse| I R -->|stabilization| L R -->|reinfection| E style S fill:#3498db,color:#fff style E fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff style L fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff style C fill:#7f8c8d,color:#fff style I fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff style T fill:#f39c12,color:#fff style R fill:#27ae60,color:#fff ``` TB deaths occur from active TB and during treatment; background mortality applies to everyone. Screening programs (Part 2) move people with active TB to treatment and people with latent infection to the cleared state. Two features of this structure carry most of the TB-specific behavior. First, **infection is not immunity**: a person with latent or cleared infection can be reinfected, but has a 79% lower risk of the disease that reinfection would otherwise cause ([Andrews et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/cir951)). The model applies this as a 79% lower probability that an exposure establishes a new infection, after which the person passes through early latency again. Rothman et al. applied this protection only to people who had recovered from TB; here it applies to everyone with prior infection, as in the cohorts it was measured in, and people who have recovered from TB have none, since disease from reinfection after cure occurs at four times the rate of new TB ([Verver et al. 2005](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.200409-1200OC)). Second, **untreated disease ends in one of three ways**: diagnosis and treatment, self-cure, or death. In the Rothman et al. model of the United States, treatment and death are the only exits from disease; in a high-burden setting the months to years of undiagnosed disease are where transmission happens. ### Age Age is continuous and advances each month. Natural history uses three bands, 0 to 4, 5 to 14, and 15 and older, because the risk of disease after infection is U-shaped in childhood: high in young children, low in school-age children, and adult-like from adolescence ([Marais et al. 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15141729/); [Martinez et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30166-5)). Children under 10 are treated as non-infectious and those 10 to 14 as half as infectious as adults, a modeling convention reflecting that childhood TB is usually paucibacillary. The contact layers use a two-group attribute, `agegrp` (`"child"` under 15, `"adult"` 15 and older), for their mixing terms. ### Contact layers | Layer | Construction | Tie duration | Contact time per adult per day | |---|---|---|---| | **household** | `netclique()` on the household id: every pair of co-residents | as long as they live together | 17.0 hours | | **regular** | TERGM with a full age-mixing matrix | mean 12 months | 6.0 hours | | **casual** | TERGM with a full age-mixing matrix | 1 month (redrawn every step) | 24.2 hours | The daily contact times are the person-hours per day that adults in the Western Cape spent with household members, repeated non-household contacts, and non-repeated contacts ([McCreesh and White 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-23797-2)). Each edge on a layer carries that layer's contact time divided by the adult mean degree on the layer, so an adult with the average number of contacts has the reported daily contact time on each layer. The probability that an edge transmits in a month is $1 - \exp(-\beta h_k m_i a_i s_j)$ for per-contact-hour risk $\beta$, monthly hours per edge $h_k$ on layer $k$, the case's individual infectiousness $m_i$ and age multiplier $a_i$, and the susceptibility $s_j$ of the other person. In the transmission probability the layers differ only in their contact time per edge; beyond that, they differ in how their ties are arranged and how long those ties last. ## Setup ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} suppressMessages(library(EpiModel)) # These are the full settings of the standalone model.R. Time steps are # months: a 50-year burn-in, then 10 years of intervention scenarios. N <- 20000 nsims <- 10 ncores <- 5 burnin <- 600 horizon <- 120 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The custom modules used in control.net() and the netclique arrival rule. # The excerpts shown under "Custom Modules" are pulled from this file. source("module-fx.R") ``` ::: ## Population and Households ### A stationary population The model runs for decades, so the population has births and deaths and its age structure has to hold still while it does. Background mortality is a step function of age, chosen so that the stationary population has a life expectancy at birth of about 60 years and about a quarter of its members under 15, close to South Africa (26% under 15). Ages are drawn from that stationary distribution, and births at a per-capita rate of $1/e_0$ keep the population's size and age structure steady in expectation, apart from TB deaths, which shrink it by a few percent over the decades of a run. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mort.breaks <- c(0, 1, 5, 15, 30, 45, 60, 70, 80) mort.rates <- c(0.025, 0.002, 0.0012, 0.004, 0.009, 0.020, 0.040, 0.080, 0.180) age_grid <- seq(0, 100 - 1 / 12, by = 1 / 12) mort_grid <- mort.rates[findInterval(age_grid, mort.breaks)] surv <- exp(-cumsum(c(0, head(mort_grid, -1) / 12))) e0 <- sum(surv) / 12 set.seed(12) age <- sample(age_grid, N, replace = TRUE, prob = surv) + runif(N, 0, 1 / 12) agegrp <- ifelse(age < 15, "child", "adult") c(life_expectancy = round(e0, 1), pct_under_15 = round(100 * mean(age < 15), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` life_expectancy pct_under_15 59.7 24.3 ``` ::: ::: ### Households with `assign_groups()` `assign_groups()`, which comes with `netclique()`, builds household ids for a population whose attributes already exist: it draws household sizes from a target distribution, places one adult in each household, puts children in the open slots of households that have an adult, and fills the rest. The size distribution below has a mean of about 3.3 people and 22% single-person households, close to South Africa's census (3.5 and 26%). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hh_size_dist <- c("1" = 0.22, "2" = 0.18, "3" = 0.17, "4" = 0.16, "5" = 0.11, "6" = 0.08, "7" = 0.05, "8" = 0.03) hh_id <- assign_groups(hh_size_dist, role = agegrp, anchor = "adult", dependent = "child") table(household_size = tabulate(hh_id)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` household_size 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 1316 1056 1027 977 637 476 314 168 ``` ::: ::: ### The household layer with `netclique()` `netclique()` turns a grouping attribute into a network layer in which every pair of nodes sharing a value is an edge. It returns an object that goes into the layer list passed to `netsim()` alongside `netest()` fits; the network resimulation skips it, and the infection module reads it with `get_edgelist()` like any other layer. Every vertex attribute the modules need is set on the one base network from which all layers are built, because `netsim()` reads nodal attributes from the first layer. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nw <- network_initialize(N) nw <- set_vertex_attribute(nw, "age", age) nw <- set_vertex_attribute(nw, "agegrp", agegrp) nw <- set_vertex_attribute(nw, "hh_id", hh_id) est_hh <- netclique(nw, group.attr = "hh_id", arrivals = "join", # <1> arrivals.FUN = newborn_household) print(est_hh, by = "agegrp") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` EpiModel Clique Network Layer ======================= Model class: netclique Grouping attribute: hh_id Layer Summary ----------------------- Nodes: 20000 Groups: 5971 Edges: 34807 Mean degree: 3.481 Isolates: 1316 Group Size Distribution ----------------------- size 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 groups 1316 1056 1027 977 637 476 314 168 Mean Degree by `agegrp` ----------------------- adult child 3.321 3.976 Arrivals: join (group chosen by arrivals.FUN) ``` ::: ::: 1. `arrivals = "join"` connects each arriving node to every member of an existing household. By default the household is drawn in proportion to its size; `arrivals.FUN` replaces that draw with a rule of our own. The arrival rule places each newborn in the household of a randomly chosen adult aged 15 to 49, so every child is born into a household with an adult of childbearing age: ```r newborn_household <- function(dat, at, new_ids, network) { active <- get_attr(dat, "active") age <- get_attr(dat, "age") hh_id <- get_attr(dat, "hh_id") parents <- setdiff(which(active == 1 & !is.na(hh_id) & age >= 15 & age < 50), new_ids) if (length(parents) == 0) { return(rep(NA, length(new_ids))) } hh_id[parents[sample.int(length(parents), length(new_ids), replace = TRUE)]] } ``` ::: {.callout-note} ## Why a clique layer, and why not a stored edgelist A household edgelist built once and passed to `netsim()` as a parameter works for a closed population over one season. With births and deaths that approach breaks. Under `tergmLite`, EpiModel deletes the departed from every attribute vector and edgelist at the end of each step and shifts the positions of everyone after them, so a stored edgelist points at the wrong people after the first death: in a test of this model's demography, half of the stored household pairs joined people in different households after 100 months. A `netclique()` layer is updated in step with the attributes. The departed leave with their edges, a household whose last member dies ceases to exist, arrivals are placed by the layer's rule, and the layer survives a restart from a saved burn-in, which Part 2 relies on. ::: ### Leaving home: `move_to_group()` Births only add people to existing households, and deaths only remove them. Left alone, households grow and their number shrinks: in a test with a similar demography and no moves, the size of the household the average person lives in rose from 4.4 to 7.1 over 50 years. People already in the population also have to change households. The `households` module (below) lets young adults leave home to form new households and moves children left without an adult into another household, both through `move_to_group()`, which sets the household id and rewires the clique layer in one step. Setting `hh_id` with `set_attr()` alone would change the attribute but leave the old household edges in place. ## Community Layers The regular and casual layers are TERGMs whose formation model is `~edges + nodemix("agegrp")`, with every cell of the child-adult mixing matrix targeted, as in the [RSV example](../rsv/). Each profile entry `a.b` is the mean number of `b`-partners per `a`-node: adults have about five regular contacts at a time and six new casual contacts each month; children have six regular contacts, mostly other children at school, and three casual contacts a month, half of them adults. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts <- table(agegrp) cells <- sub("^mix\\.agegrp\\.", "", names(summary(nw ~ nodemix("agegrp", levels2 = TRUE)))) mix_targets <- function(profile) { out <- setNames(numeric(length(cells)), cells) for (nm in names(profile)) { ab <- strsplit(nm, ".", fixed = TRUE)[[1]] n_a <- as.numeric(counts[ab[1]]) e <- if (ab[1] == ab[2]) n_a * profile[[nm]] / 2 else n_a * profile[[nm]] cell <- paste(sort(ab), collapse = ".") out[cell] <- out[cell] + e } pmax(round(out), 1) } reg_profile <- c(adult.adult = 4.6, child.adult = 1.0, child.child = 5.0) cas_profile <- c(adult.adult = 5.5, child.adult = 1.5, child.child = 1.5) reg_targets <- mix_targets(reg_profile) cas_targets <- mix_targets(cas_profile) formation <- ~edges + nodemix("agegrp", levels2 = -1) san_ctrl <- control.ergm(SAN = control.san(SAN.maxit = 20, SAN.nsteps = 2^21)) d.rate <- 1 / e0 / 12 est_reg <- netest(nw, formation, target.stats = c(sum(reg_targets), as.numeric(reg_targets[-1])), coef.diss = dissolution_coefs(~offset(edges), duration = 12, # <1> d.rate = d.rate), set.control.ergm = san_ctrl, verbose = FALSE) est_cas <- netest(nw, formation, target.stats = c(sum(cas_targets), as.numeric(cas_targets[-1])), coef.diss = dissolution_coefs(~offset(edges), duration = 1), # <2> set.control.ergm = san_ctrl, verbose = FALSE) ``` ::: 1. Regular ties last 12 months on average. `d.rate` adjusts the dissolution coefficient for ties that end because a partner dies. 2. Casual ties last one month: every step brings a new set. ### Simulating the community layers faithfully `tergm` simulates each time step with a Markov chain whose default length is far too short for these two layers. With the default chain, about half of the casual ties survived from one month to the next, although the model says every casual tie lasts one month, and the regular layer's children-with-children cell settled about 20% below its target, because proposals rarely land on the small set of child-child dyads. Both problems largely go away with a chain long enough to visit every tie, which scales with the number of edges and hence with `N`: carried-over casual ties fall to about 3% a month. The longer chains about double the time spent simulating the two layers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc <- function(steps) { control.simulate.formula.tergm(MCMC.burnin.min = steps, MCMC.burnin.max = steps) } tergm_persist <- mcmc(20 * N) tergm_redraw <- mcmc(25 * N) ``` ::: ### Diagnostics and contact time The regular layer is simulated dynamically, which checks both its degree by age group and its mean tie duration; the casual layer's ties last one step, so its formation model is checked with static simulations. The household layer's degree is read directly from the cliques. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dx_reg <- netdx(est_reg, nsims = 2, nsteps = 60, set.control.tergm = tergm_persist, nwstats.formula = ~edges + nodefactor("agegrp", levels = TRUE), verbose = FALSE) dx_cas <- netdx(est_cas, nsims = 10, dynamic = FALSE, nwstats.formula = ~edges + nodefactor("agegrp", levels = TRUE), verbose = FALSE) 4.92| 6.00| 4.90| 5.95| |casual | 5.98| 3.00| 5.94| 2.99| ::: ::: Contact time converts degree into exposure. McCreesh and White (2018) report that adults in the Western Cape spent about 17.0 person-hours a day with household members, 6.0 with repeated non-household contacts, and 24.2 with non-repeated contacts. Dividing each by the adult mean degree on its layer gives the monthly hours carried by one edge: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hours_day <- c(household = 17.0, regular = 6.0, casual = 24.2) layer_hours <- hours_day / deg_tbl[, "adult"] * 365.25 / 12 round(layer_hours, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` household regular casual 155.8 37.1 123.1 ``` ::: ::: A household edge carries 156 hours a month, about 5.1 hours a day with each co-resident; a regular edge 37 hours; a casual edge 123. A casual edge is an abstraction: the roughly 240 people an adult meets briefly in a month, in the Western Cape survey, are pooled into about six edges that are replaced every month. That reproduces the total casual contact time and the fact that it is spent with ever-changing people, but an edge can transmit only once in a month, so the pooling caps how many people a highly infectious case can infect through casual contact. The Simplifications callout below says what that does to the results. ## Custom Modules Nine custom modules run in each monthly step: `init_tb` (one-shot setup of the TB states), `aging`, `infect`, `progress` (natural history and passive diagnosis), `screen` (the Part 2 programs), `deaths`, `births`, `households` (leaving home), and `tally` (summary counts). Full code is in `module-fx.R`; the parts that carry the model's logic are below. ### `infect`: transmission weighted by contact time, on every layer The module walks each layer's current edgelist, whether the layer is a clique or a TERGM, and gives each discordant edge its own probability of transmission. Nothing downstream of `get_edgelist()` depends on the kind of layer. ```r infness[ids_i] <- inf_mult[ids_i] * # <1> age.mult[findInterval(age[ids_i], age.breaks)] sus[status == "s"] <- 1 # <2> sus[status %in% c("l", "c")] <- sus.latent sus[status == "r"] <- sus.recovered for (k in seq_along(hours)) { if (hours[k] == 0) next el <- get_edgelist(dat, network = k) # <3> a <- el[, 1] b <- el[, 2] fwd <- infness[a] > 0 & sus[b] > 0 rev <- infness[b] > 0 & sus[a] > 0 inf <- c(a[fwd], b[rev]) rec <- c(b[fwd], a[rev]) p <- 1 - exp(-beta * hours[k] * infness[inf] * sus[rec]) # <4> hit <- which(runif(length(p)) < p) if (length(hit) > 0) { del <- rbind(del, data.frame(sus = rec[hit], inf = inf[hit], layer = k)) } } del <- del[sample.int(nrow(del)), , drop = FALSE] # <5> del <- del[!duplicated(del$sus), , drop = FALSE] ``` 1. **Infectiousness.** Each case's multiplier `inf_mult` is drawn when the episode begins, from a gamma distribution with mean 1 and shape `inf.k = 0.15`; the age multiplier is 0 under 10, 0.5 at 10 to 14, and 1 from 15. 2. **Susceptibility.** Full for the never infected and for people who have recovered from TB; 0.21 for people with latent or cleared infection. 3. **One call for any layer.** Layer 1 is the `netclique` layer, layers 2 and 3 the TERGMs; in the Part 1 variant with redrawn households a fourth layer is added and the clique layer's hours are set to zero. 4. **Contact-hour dose.** The probability rises with contact time and saturates: an edge cannot transmit more than once, however long or intense the contact. 5. **Competing exposures.** A node infected on several edges in the same step is infected once, and its infector, and so its layer, is drawn at random among the successes. The transmission record keeps the layer, both ages, the recipient's prior state, and the infector's unique id, from which the concentration of transmission among cases is computed. ### `progress`: competing risks at a monthly step Most TB states have more than one exit. The module draws whether a node leaves a state in the month from the sum of the exit rates, and then which exit in proportion to the rates, so the share of people taking each route is exact at a monthly step rather than depending on the order in which transitions are checked. ```r exits <- function(ids, rates) { rates <- matrix(rates, nrow = length(ids)) tot <- rowSums(rates) out <- integer(length(ids)) go <- which(u1[ids] < 1 - exp(-tot / 12)) # <1> if (length(go) > 0) { out[go] <- 1L cum <- 0 for (j in seq_len(ncol(rates) - 1)) { # <2> cum <- cum + rates[go, j] / tot[go] out[go] <- out[go] + (u2[ids[go]] > cum) } } out } ## early latent: progression or stabilization, by age band ids <- which(active == 1 & status0 == "e" & infTime < at) x <- exits(ids, cbind(prog.early[band[ids]], stab.early[band[ids]])) ## active TB: diagnosis, TB death, or self-cure ids <- which(active == 1 & status0 == "i") x <- exits(ids, cbind(diag.rate, tb.mort[band[ids]], self.cure)) ``` 1. Annual rates are converted to a monthly probability of leaving the state. 2. The exit taken is drawn in proportion to the rates. ### `screen`: one package for household and random screening Household contact investigation and the equal-effort random arm deliver the same package, so it is written once. Screened people with active TB are found with an age-specific sensitivity and start treatment; eligible people who are not found to have TB are offered preventive therapy (TPT), and a completed course clears early or late latent infection. ```r package <- function(ids, status, txTime, dxTime) { sens <- ifelse(age[ids] < 15, screen.sens[1], screen.sens[2]) found <- ids[status[ids] == "i" & runif(length(ids)) < sens] status[found] <- "t" txTime[found] <- at dxTime[found] <- at elig <- setdiff(ids[age[ids] < tpt.age.max & status[ids] != "t"], found) started <- elig[runif(length(elig)) < tpt.start] completed <- started[runif(length(started)) < tpt.complete] latent <- completed[status[completed] %in% c("e", "l")] # <1> cleared <- latent[runif(length(latent)) < tpt.eff] status[cleared] <- "c" ... } index <- which(is_active & !is.na(dxTime) & dxTime == at) # <2> idx_hh <- unique(hh_id[index]) contacts <- setdiff(which(is_active & hh_id %in% idx_hh & !is.na(hh_id)), index) reached_hh <- idx_hh[runif(length(idx_hh)) < hhci.reach] # <3> ev <- contacts[hh_id[contacts] %in% reached_hh & status[contacts] != "t"] ev <- ev[runif(length(ev)) < hhci.eval] out <- package(ev, status, txTime, dxTime) ``` 1. TPT acts only on people who are infected, but it is offered without testing for infection, as WHO recommends for household contacts under 5 and allows for older contacts. A cleared infection keeps the partial protection of prior infection; TPT adds none of its own, so a treated contact can be reinfected. 2. Index cases are everyone diagnosed in this step, whether passively or by a screening program. 3. The household id makes "the co-residents of a newly diagnosed person" a set the module can find directly. The module also records, for every index case, the state of each co-resident at the moment of diagnosis. That is the model's counterpart of the household contact studies used to check it below, and it is recorded in every scenario whether or not a program is running. ### `households`: leaving home with `move_to_group()` ```r elig <- which(active == 1 & !is.na(hh_id) & age >= leave.ages[1] & age < leave.ages[2] & size >= 3 & adults >= 2) leavers <- elig[runif(length(elig)) < leave.rate] if (length(leavers) > 0) { leavers <- leavers[sample.int(length(leavers))] new_ids <- max(hh_id, na.rm = TRUE) + ceiling(seq_along(leavers) / 2) # <1> dat <- move_to_group(dat, ids = leavers, group = new_ids) # <2> hh_id <- get_attr(dat, "hh_id") } ``` 1. Leavers are paired at random into new two-person households, and an odd leaver lives alone. Unused ids start new households. 2. `move_to_group()` removes each mover's household edges and connects the mover to every member of the new household, including the partner who moved with them. The same function moves children whose household has no one aged 15 or older left, together, into the household of a randomly chosen adult. ### `births`: append every attribute ```r dat <- append_core_attr(dat, at, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "status", "s", n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "age", 0, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "agegrp", "child", n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "hh_id", NA, n_new) # <1> dat <- append_attr(dat, "infTime", NA_integer_, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "infType", NA_character_, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "inf_mult", NA_real_, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "txTime", NA_integer_, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "dxTime", NA_integer_, n_new) dat <- append_attr(dat, "hhcTime", NA_integer_, n_new) ``` 1. The household is left missing here and set by the clique layer's arrival rule, `newborn_household()`, when `nwupdate` adds the new nodes to the layers. Every attribute a module reads must be appended for arrivals. Leaving out `status` or `infTime` stops the simulation with an error, but leaving out any other attribute does not: EpiModel fills it for the new nodes with values sampled from the current population, which would give newborns a random infectiousness multiplier, treatment start, or contact history without any warning. The arrival rule of a `netclique()` layer (its `arrivals.FUN` argument) is a different function from the arrivals module given to `control.net()` (also called `arrivals.FUN`): the module creates the new nodes, and the rule then places them on the clique layer. ### Module order EpiModel's default order runs user-supplied modules with nonstandard names before the built-in ones, which here would run `households` before `nwupdate` has added the newborns to the layers. The order is set explicitly: ``` resim_nets -> summary_nets -> initTB -> aging -> infection -> progress -> screen -> departures -> arrivals -> nwupdate -> households -> tally -> prevalence ``` Infection runs before progression, and `progress` requires `infTime < at` for the exit from early latency, so every infection spends at least one month there. `screen` runs after `progress`, so that the index cases of a step are the people diagnosed in that step. ## Parameters **Latency and progression.** The share of infections that progress to disease during early latency is 15% under 5, 5% at ages 5 to 14, and 10% from 15. The childhood values follow the age pattern of the pre-chemotherapy literature, in which infection in the first two years of life often progressed and infection at ages 2 to 10 rarely did ([Marais et al. 2004](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15141729/)). They sit below the 19% (8 to 37%) two-year risk in infected contacts under 5 in a meta-analysis of child contacts ([Martinez et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30166-5)) and well below the risks in a low-incidence contact cohort (56% under 5 and 28% at 5 to 14; [Trauer et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2015.11.017)), values that would make children an implausibly large share of incident TB in this model; the adult value lies between the 5% of a model fitted to contact-tracing data ([Ragonnet et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epidem.2017.06.002)) and the 14% five-year risk estimated for England and Wales ([Vynnycky and Fine 1997](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0950268897007917)). The stabilization rates, which set how long early latency lasts, are Ragonnet's: a mean of about 2 to 3 months in children and 5 to 6 months in adults. Late reactivation (0.12% a year in adults) is Ragonnet's, and late latent infection clears at 2.8% a year ([Emery et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2020.1635)). Rothman et al. derived a comparable structure from a two-year mean stay in fast latency, with about 5.5% of new infections in U.S.-born adults progressing within five years, below the 11.5 to 14.5% seen within about four and a half years among recently infected contacts ([Trauer et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chest.2015.11.017)); the adult value here sits closer to the contact data. **Active disease and treatment.** Undiagnosed TB is diagnosed at a rate of 1.0 a year and self-cures at 0.15 a year. It kills adults at 0.10 a year, so that an untreated adult case lasts about 4 years and 40% end in death, between the 10-year case fatality of untreated smear-positive (70%) and smear-negative (20%) TB ([Tiemersma et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0017601)). For children the rates, 0.12 a year under 5 and 0.03 at 5 to 14, give untreated case fatalities of 44% and 17%, close to the 44% and 15% reported for those ages in the pre-treatment era ([Jenkins et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(16)30474-1)). Treatment lasts six months, with 3.5% dying during treatment and 93% of the rest cured; the others return to active TB. People who recover relapse at 2.4% a year while their risk lasts, a mean of two years before stabilizing into late latent infection ([Vega et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1136/thoraxjnl-2020-215449)). **Transmission and what was tuned.** The per-contact-hour probability $\beta$ was chosen by iterating the baseline so that incidence lands near 400 per 100,000 a year, a level typical of high-burden countries (WHO estimates for 2024: South Africa 389 and Indonesia 382 per 100,000); the runs used to choose it spanned about 300 to 550 across simulations. Two other choices were revised once after a first full run: the childhood progression risks and TB mortality were lowered because children made up almost a fifth of incident TB and deaths were about 15% of cases, both above the ranges WHO estimates. The leaving-home rate was tuned to keep household sizes steady. The contact time on each layer, the dispersion of infectiousness (`inf.k = 0.15`, estimated from the sizes of genotypic clusters in Cape Town by [McCreesh and White 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-23797-2)), and the 79% protection of prior infection were set from the literature and not adjusted, and the contact profiles were chosen to be plausible rather than fitted. The household share of transmission was never a target; it is an output, although, as the Simplifications callout explains, the way casual contact is pooled into a few edges pushes it up. **Programs.** Household contact investigation reaches 65% of index households and evaluates 85% of their members; screening detects active TB with a sensitivity of 0.8 in adults and 0.7 in children; 85% of eligible contacts start TPT, 80% of them complete it, and a completed course clears infection in 90% (3HP completion in trials was 82% in adults and 88% in children; [Sterling et al. 2011](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1104875); [Villarino et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2014.3158)). TPT is given to contacts of every age in one arm and to contacts under 5, WHO's strong recommendation, in another. Community-wide screening follows the ACT3 trial in Vietnam ([Marks et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1902129)): an annual round that tests 42% of people aged 15 and older, about the share of adults who gave sputum for testing in each ACT3 round, and detects active TB with a sensitivity of 0.85, with no TPT. TPT gives no lasting protection in the model, in line with the rapid loss of protection after mass preventive therapy in a high-transmission setting ([Churchyard et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1214289)). ::: {.callout-important} ## Simplifications - **No HIV.** In Southern Africa more than half of incident TB is in people with HIV, and TB there cannot be understood without it. The setting here is a generic high-burden one without HIV; adding an HIV attribute that raises progression and mortality is the first extension. - **One infectious state.** Active TB is not split into subclinical and clinical disease, or smear-positive and smear-negative. Subclinical TB, which is common, infectious, and never diagnosed passively, is what screening finds that passive case finding misses, and it would favor the screening arms. - **No sex.** Adult men carry most TB transmission in high-burden settings. - **Casual contact pooled into a few edges.** An adult's casual contact time is carried by about six edges a month rather than by the roughly 240 people a month in the Western Cape survey, because a TERGM with that many edges would be slow to simulate. An edge transmits at most once a month, so the pooling caps how many people a highly infectious case can infect through casual contact, and it pushes the household share of transmission up. In a smaller test (N = 5,000, three simulations each), four times as many casual edges with a quarter of the hours each lowered the household share of adults' infections from about 16% to 13% and of children's from about 42% to 32%. - **Contact time as the only difference between layers.** A contact-hour carries the same risk at home, at work, and on a minibus. Ventilation differs by setting, and the per-hour risk in crowded, poorly ventilated public places could be higher or lower than at home. - **TPT acts immediately.** A course is completed or not at the moment it is offered; in reality 3HP takes three months, during which some recently infected contacts progress. - **No drug resistance, no BCG, no costs.** ::: ### Parameter provenance | Parameter | Incidence over the last 20 years of the burn-in averaged 450 (95% Monte Carlo interval 368 to 532) per 100,000 a year, around the 400 used to choose $\beta$. Of incident TB, 16.7% was in children, 83.3% was diagnosed and treated, and 10.5% ended in death, to be compared with the WHO estimates in the table. The rows that depend on contact structure were not targets. Adults acquired 15.2% of their infections at home, although households hold 36% of adults' contact time; molecular and genomic studies attribute 8 to 19% of disease to household transmission, and McCreesh and White's model 13%. Those are shares of disease rather than of infections, but in this model the two differ little among adults, whose risk of disease after infection does not depend on where they were infected. The most infectious 20% of cases caused 89.5% of infections. Household contacts had active TB at the moment the index case was diagnosed 3.8% of the time, and 2.8% developed TB within the next two years; among contacts under 5, 9.1% had TB at the investigation or within two years, against 7.6% in the child-contact meta-analysis. The mean household size was 3.43, with 19.5% of households a single person: the leaving-home moves hold the household structure near where it started. Two rows are off, each in an instructive way: - **Children acquire more of their infections at home** (39.7%) than the 10 to 30% of the population-attributable estimates ([Martinez et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwx025); [Martinez et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/S2213-2600(19)30137-7)), and closer to the 44 to 58% attributed to household exposure among children who live with a case ([Zelner et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwu192)). Part of the gap comes from pooling casual contact into a few edges (see the Simplifications callout), and part from children here having few non-household contacts with adults, while real children are also exposed on transport, at clinics, at school, and in other households ([Andrews et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/infdis/jiu138)). - **Household contacts are more often infected** (76.3%, counting latent, cleared, and past infection) than the 45 to 52% found in contact studies, where tests also miss some past infection. Adults in this model accumulate infection over a lifetime of heavy exposure: 64.5% of those aged 15 to 34 have been infected. ### Contact time is not transmission ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cols_st <- c(baseline = "black", regular_redrawn = "#e67e22", household_redrawn = "#c0392b") annual <- function(sim, vars, rows) { yr <- ceiling(seq_along(rows) / 12) ev <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(vars, function(v) as.matrix(sim$epi[[v]])[rows, , drop = FALSE])) pop <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(c("num.child", "num.adult"), function(v) as.matrix(sim$epi[[v]])[rows, , drop = FALSE])) sapply(split(seq_along(rows), yr), function(i) { mean(1e5 * colSums(ev[i, , drop = FALSE]) / colMeans(pop[i, , drop = FALSE])) }) } inc_all <- c(inc_vars("child"), inc_vars("adult")) ``` ::: The layer shares and the incidence of each structure are summarized per simulation over the same 20-year window: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Structure summaries"} struct_summary <- function(sim, rows) { layers <- sim$param$layer.names inf_l <- sapply(layers, function(l) { epi_sum(sim, paste0("inf.", l, c(".child", ".adult")), rows) }) inf_l <- matrix(inf_l, ncol = length(layers), dimnames = list(NULL, layers)) c_ <- calib(sim, rows) half <- split(rows, seq_along(rows) > length(rows) / 2) out <- list( inc = c_$inc, inc_child = c_$inc_child, inc_adult = c_$inc_adult, drift = 100 * (calib(sim, half[[2]])$inc / calib(sim, half[[1]])$inc - Two features of the network produce the gap, and neither is a parameter that says households transmit less: 1. **Saturation of persistent ties.** A person with TB meets the same few co-residents month after month. Once they are infected, and in this setting many already were before the case began, further contact produces little new infection: reinfection of someone with prior infection is 79% less likely to succeed, and someone in early latency or with TB cannot be infected again. An edge can transmit only once, and a household edge stays the same edge for years; casual contact brings new people every month. 2. **Overdispersion.** With `inf.k = 0.15`, about 40% of cases have less than 1% of the average infectiousness and transmit almost nothing anywhere, while a few are many times more infectious than average. A highly infectious case infects most of its household within months, and the rest of its transmission goes to its regular and casual contacts. The regular layer, persistent but open (a coworker's own contacts are mostly not the case's), gives adults 15% of their infections for 13% of their contact time. ### The persistence of ties ::: {#tbl-structures .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::kable(struct_tbl, col.names = c("Structure", "Incidence", "Change from baseline (%)", "Children", "Adults", "Household (%)", "Regular (%)", "Casual (%)", "Reinfections (%)"), caption = "TB incidence per 100,000 per year (all ages, children, adults), the percent change in all-ages incidence from the baseline, the share of all infections transmitted on each layer, and the share of infections that were reinfections, over the last 20 years of burn-in; mean (95% Monte Carlo interval). Community-wide screening of adults averted 44.2% (95% Monte Carlo interval 28.7 to 59.7) of incident TB over 10 years. ACT3 measured prevalence rather than incidence: after three annual rounds, adult prevalence in the screened communities was 0.56 times that in the control communities ([Marks et al. 2019](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1902129)), and the model's ratio of adult prevalence in year 4 to that under passive case finding was 0.43 (95% Monte Carlo interval 0.30 to 0.56). Household investigation averted 14.6% (95% Monte Carlo interval 3.8 to 25.4) without TPT, 22.3% (95% Monte Carlo interval 6.1 to 38.5) with TPT for contacts under 5, and 24.6% (95% Monte Carlo interval 8.3 to 41.0) with TPT for contacts of all ages; the random arm, with the same effort and the same package as the last, averted 6.3% (95% Monte Carlo interval -12.2 to 24.7). With 10 simulations, all three of the household arms have an effect distinguishable from zero, and the random arm's effect is not. The spread of the points in the figure is the reason to read these rows with their intervals. This model sits where small changes in transmission move incidence a lot: in Part 1, rearranging the same contact hours changed incidence by as much as 52%, and each active case a program finds early averts further cases over the rest of the decade (next section). The population effects of programs that find a few percent of cases early therefore vary widely between simulations, even though every scenario starts from the same state, and 10 simulations do not pin them down. Prior models place the population effect of household contact tracing at 4 to 27% over five years ([Kasaie et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1164/rccm.201310-1846OC); [Havumaki et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0293519)). ### Yield and the direct protection of contacts The programs' own outcomes are measured on the people they reach and vary much less between simulations than population incidence. ::: {#tbl-program .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Program yield. Comparing any program with passive case finding would also credit it with its effect on transmission, which lowers every contact's risk: the community-wide arm, which gives no TPT and investigates no households, lowers household contacts' risk too. TPT reduced the two-year risk of TB among contacts under 5 by 33%, at 32 completed courses per case averted, and among contacts 5 and older by 29%, at 48 courses per case averted. Fewer courses are needed for young children because their risk of disease after infection is higher. In Lima, preventive therapy for household contacts with a positive skin test prevented about 30 cases per 1,000 courses ([Zelner et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyx171)); the model offers TPT without testing, so part of every course goes to a contact who is not infected. Extending TPT from children under 5 to contacts of all ages added about 4,985 completed courses per 100,000 over the decade, which at that rate prevents about 104 cases per 100,000 directly, 1.9% of incident TB. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The most a household program could prevent directly: the share of all # incident TB, under passive case finding, that occurs in people identified # as a household contact in the previous 24 months contact_share <- 100 * (oc$none$contact_tb_u5 + oc$none$contact_tb_5p) / epi_sum(sims$none, c(inc_vars("child"), inc_vars("adult")), rows_c) fmt(mc(contact_share), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "12.5 (11.6, 13.4)" ``` ::: ::: Under passive case finding, 12.5% of all incident TB occurred in people who had been household contacts of a newly diagnosed case in the previous two years. That is the most a household program could prevent directly, even with complete coverage and perfect TPT. Whatever it achieves beyond that comes indirectly, by finding infectious people earlier and so shortening the time in which they transmit, most of it outside the household. This is the network's account of why household contact investigation is efficient for the people it reaches but limited in what it can do directly for the population. In the ZAMSTAR trial in Zambia and South Africa, communities randomized to a household-based intervention had 18% lower TB prevalence, with a confidence interval that included no effect (prevalence ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.04; [Ayles et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(13)61131-9)). ### Between-simulation variability ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cv <- sapply(st, function(x) sd(x$inc) / mean(x$inc)) round(cv, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` baseline regular_redrawn household_redrawn 0.25 0.28 0.27 ``` ::: ::: The coefficient of variation of incidence across the 10 baseline simulations, each averaged over 20 years, is 0.25. Two features of the model produce this much variation: transmission is concentrated in a few highly infectious cases, and the population of 20,000 has on average only 77 people with undiagnosed active TB at a time. More simulations narrow the intervals in proportion to the square root of their number, and a larger population narrows them further, at a cost in run time that grows with both. Resuming each burn-in state several times with different random numbers is a cheaper way to tighten the Part 2 comparisons, since most of their noise arises after the programs start. ## Next Steps - **HIV.** Add a fixed or dynamic HIV attribute that multiplies progression, reactivation, and TB mortality, with antiretroviral therapy reducing them. This is what a Southern African TB model needs first, and it would also make household clustering of HIV, and so of TB risk, a network question. - **Subclinical TB.** Split active TB into subclinical and clinical states with transitions both ways, so that screening finds people passive case finding never would. The community-wide arm would gain the most. - **Sex and heterogeneous contact.** Give adult men more casual contact time, and let casual degree vary between people rather than only between age groups; the non-repeated contacts in the Western Cape survey had a variance twelve times their mean. - **Where contact happens.** Weight contact-hours by the ventilation of the setting (households, transport, workplaces, clinics), so that per-hour risk differs between layers. Model conclusions about the household share are sensitive to the ratio of per-hour risk in public places to that at home. - **Contact investigation beyond the household.** Turning on the cumulative edgelist (`cumulative.edgelist = TRUE` in `control.net()`, with `truncate.el.cuml` at least as long as the lookback) would record the regular layer's partnerships, so that each index case's regular contacts over a lookback window could be investigated with `get_partners()`; see the [contact tracing example](../seir-contact-tracing/). - **More casual edges.** Raise the casual layer's degree and lower its hours per edge toward the hundreds of brief contacts a month in the Western Cape survey, with the TERGM chain lengthened in proportion, and see how far the household share falls. - **More replicates for Part 2.** Resume each burn-in state several times with different random numbers to tighten the program comparisons, whose noise arises mostly after the programs start. - **TPT with a duration.** Hold contacts in a treatment state for the three months of 3HP, during which recently infected contacts can still progress, and add an effect on reinfection during the course. - **A prevention-of-disease vaccine.** Rothman et al. (2026) targeted a vaccine by clinical risk group in the United States; in this network it could be targeted by exposure, to household contacts of newly diagnosed people, and compared with vaccinating the same number of people at random. - **Matched-incidence comparisons.** Part 1 compares contact structures at fixed per-hour risk.
